ATL.formerly: Tri-Cities Blackhawks, Milwaukee Hawks, St. Louis Hawks
ATL.nickname: The franchise that keeps almost getting there
ATL.identity: One of the league's oldest franchises, the Hawks won their only title in St. Louis in 1958 behind Bob Pettit. In Atlanta they've mostly been a solid playoff team without a deep run. Dominique Wilkins' dunk contests in the '80s, a surprise 60-win season in 2015 and an unexpected trip to the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals are the high points.

BOS.identity: The NBA's winningest franchise with 18 championships. Bill Russell's Celtics won 11 titles in 13 years, Larry Bird's '80s teams fought the Lakers for the decade, and the 2008 'Big Three' and the 2024 team added more banners. In Boston the expectation is the title, every year.

BKN.formerly: New Jersey Americans, New York Nets (ABA), New Jersey Nets
BKN.nickname: Brooklyn's team, still looking for a first NBA title
BKN.identity: The Nets won two ABA titles with Dr. J before joining the NBA, then spent decades in New Jersey. Jason Kidd took them to two straight Finals (2002, 2003). Since moving to Brooklyn in 2012 they've been through big-name experiments (Garnett and Pierce, then Durant, Irving and Harden) that never won a title, and full rebuilds after each.

CHA.nickname: Teal, purple and a long playoff drought
CHA.identity: The original Hornets were a '90s cult favorite (Larry Johnson, Alonzo Mourning, 5'3" Muggsy Bogues) before moving to New Orleans. Charlotte got an expansion team, the Bobcats, in 2004, once owned by Michael Jordan, and took back the Hornets name and history in 2014. Winning a playoff series has been rare.

CHI.identity: Michael Jordan, Scottie Pippen and coach Phil Jackson won six titles in eight years, the most famous dynasty in sports. The 1995-96 team went 72-10. Derrick Rose became the youngest MVP in 2011. Since then Chicago has been stuck in the middle of the league.

CLE.identity: Cleveland's identity is tied to LeBron James, the Akron kid they drafted in 2003. He left for Miami, came back, and in 2016 led a comeback from 3-1 down in the Finals against the 73-win Warriors, ending the city's 52-year championship drought. The four straight Finals against Golden State (2015–18) are their defining era.

DAL.identity: Dirk Nowitzki spent 21 seasons in Dallas and his 2011 title run over LeBron's Heat is the franchise's crowning moment. Luka Dončić took them back to the Finals in 2024, then the team traded him to the Lakers in February 2025, one of the most shocking trades in league history. Fans still haven't forgiven it.

DEN.nickname: Mile-high altitude and a passing center
DEN.identity: Denver was a fun ABA and run-and-gun team for decades but rarely a real contender. That changed with Nikola Jokić, a second-round pick from Serbia who became a three-time MVP and led them to their first title in 2023. Playing at 5,280 feet tires out visiting teams.

DET.identity: The 'Bad Boys' of Isiah Thomas and Bill Laimbeer won back-to-back titles with physical, sometimes dirty defense. The 2004 team won it all without a superstar, beating the Kobe and Shaq Lakers. After a long dark stretch, including a 28-game losing streak in 2023-24, Detroit rebuilt and is relevant again.

GS.nickname: The team that changed basketball with the three
GS.identity: Stephen Curry's Warriors made the three-pointer the center of the modern game and won four titles between 2015 and 2022, adding Kevin Durant for two of them. They set the regular-season record (73-9) in 2016 and then blew a 3-1 Finals lead to Cleveland. Earlier history includes Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game, which he scored as a Philadelphia Warrior.

HOU.identity: Hakeem Olajuwon led back-to-back titles in the '90s while Jordan was away. Yao Ming made Houston huge in China. James Harden's analytics-driven teams took nearly every shot as a three or a layup and came within one game of the 2018 Finals. After a rebuild they're a young, defense-first team again.

IND.nickname: Basketball-crazy Indiana, still chasing an NBA ring
IND.identity: The Pacers dominated the ABA with three titles but have none in the NBA. Reggie Miller's late-game shooting against the Knicks is their lore. They reached the Finals in 2000 and again in 2025, when they took OKC to Game 7 but lost after Tyrese Haliburton tore his Achilles in that game.

LAC.identity: For decades the Clippers were the league's punchline. 'Lob City' with Chris Paul and Blake Griffin made them fun, and owner Steve Ballmer has spent big since, bringing in Kawhi Leonard and Paul George and building his own arena, the Intuit Dome. They've never reached the Finals.

LAL.identity: 17 titles across every era: George Mikan in Minneapolis, Jerry West and Wilt, 'Showtime' with Magic and Kareem, the Shaq and Kobe three-peat, Kobe's two with Pau Gasol, and LeBron's 2020 bubble title. Stars want to play here, and anything short of a title counts as a failure. Their rivalry with Boston is the league's oldest grudge.

MEM.identity: Born in Vancouver and moved to Memphis in 2001. The 'Grit and Grind' era (Marc Gasol, Zach Randolph, Tony Allen, Mike Conley) won with physical defense and made the 2013 Western Conference Finals. Since then they've been a young, loud team that talks a lot of trash.

MIA.identity: Pat Riley built a famously demanding culture: the fittest players, the hardest workers, no excuses. Dwyane Wade and Shaq won in 2006; then LeBron's 'Decision' to join Wade and Bosh produced four straight Finals and two titles. They regularly beat bigger-name teams in the playoffs, like reaching the 2023 Finals as an 8th seed.

MIL.identity: Young Kareem (then Lew Alcindor) and Oscar Robertson won a title in the franchise's third season. Fifty years later Giannis Antetokounmpo, a skinny unknown drafted 15th out of Greece, grew into a two-time MVP and scored 50 in the closeout game of the 2021 Finals. Milwaukee is a small market that rarely lands stars any other way.

MIN.identity: Kevin Garnett carried Minnesota for 12 seasons and reached the 2004 Western Conference Finals. Then came a long drought of lottery picks and bad luck. Recently they've become a real threat, making back-to-back Western Conference Finals in 2024 and 2025.

NO.nickname: Big Easy, big potential, lots of injuries
NO.identity: The Hornets moved from Charlotte in 2002 and became the Pelicans in 2013. After Hurricane Katrina they played two seasons mostly in Oklahoma City. Chris Paul and later Anthony Davis were stars who eventually asked to leave. Recent teams have been talented but injury-wrecked.

NY.identity: Willis Reed limping out for Game 7 in 1970 is Knicks lore. Their two titles came in the early '70s. Patrick Ewing's rough '90s teams had famous wars with the Bulls, Pacers and Heat but never won. Then came decades of dysfunction before a revival, including the 2025 Eastern Conference Finals, their first since 2000. MSG is the most famous arena in the sport.

OKC.nickname: Young, deep and drafted to perfection
OKC.identity: The franchise moved from Seattle in 2008 (Sonics fans are still angry). Kevin Durant, Russell Westbrook and James Harden were a young dynasty that broke up too soon. GM Sam Presti then stockpiled draft picks and built around Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, winning the 2025 title with one of the youngest championship teams ever. The 1979 title came in Seattle.

ORL.identity: Orlando won the draft lottery twice in a row in the early '90s. Shaq and Penny Hardaway made the 1995 Finals, then Shaq left for LA. Dwight Howard took them to the 2009 Finals. Since then they've been a long-armed, defense-first team built through the draft.

PHI.identity: Wilt Chamberlain's 1967 team and the 'Fo, Fo, Fo' 1983 team (Dr. J and Moses Malone) won titles. Allen Iverson carried them to the 2001 Finals. 'The Process' was a years-long deliberate tank for top draft picks; it produced Joel Embiid, but repeated second-round exits made playoff heartbreak the theme.

PHX.identity: Possibly the best franchise never to win a title. Finals trips in 1976, 1993 (Barkley's MVP year) and 2021 all ended in losses, and Steve Nash's fast-paced 'Seven Seconds or Less' teams of the mid-2000s never got there. Recent years were an expensive superstar experiment.

POR.identity: Bill Walton's 1977 title sparked 'Blazermania', and the fans have stayed fiercely loyal since. Clyde Drexler's teams made two Finals in the early '90s. Damian Lillard's long-range buzzer-beaters defined the 2010s. Now in a youth rebuild.

SAC.formerly: Rochester Royals, Cincinnati Royals, Kansas City Kings
SAC.identity: The oldest franchise in the league by roots, with a title back in Rochester in 1951. The early-2000s Kings (Webber, Divac, Peja, Bibby) were beautiful to watch and lost a controversial 2002 Western Conference Finals to the Lakers. A record 16-year playoff drought ended in 2023; they light a purple laser beam after every home win.

SA.nickname: Quiet dynasty, now the Wemby era
SA.identity: The Spurs won five titles with Tim Duncan and coach Gregg Popovich through steady, unselfish team play and smart international scouting (Manu Ginóbili, Tony Parker). Their 2014 ball movement is still studied. Now they're built around Victor Wembanyama, a 7'4" French phenom unlike anyone before.

TOR.identity: The only Canadian team. Vince Carter's dunks put them on the map. The Lowry and DeRozan era made them consistently good, and a one-year trade for Kawhi Leonard won the 2019 title, sealed by his four-bounce buzzer-beater against Philadelphia. The fans and celebrity superfan Drake are famously loud.

UTAH.identity: John Stockton and Karl Malone ran the pick-and-roll together for 18 seasons and reached back-to-back Finals in 1997 and 1998, losing both to Jordan's Bulls. The 'Jazz' name made sense in New Orleans and was kept after the move to Salt Lake City. The crowd is one of the loudest in the league.

WSH.formerly: Chicago Packers, Baltimore Bullets, Washington Bullets
WSH.identity: The Bullets of Wes Unseld and Elvin Hayes won the 1978 title. The team became the Wizards in 1997, and Michael Jordan came out of retirement to play here (2001–03). John Wall and Bradley Beal's teams never made it past the second round. Now in a full rebuild.
